title: The sabbath idea
hookLine: Judaism's weekly day of rest, rooted in creation and the commandments (Genesis 2:2–3; Exodus 20:8–11)

cards: It's Friday, just before sunset, in a Jewish home. The cooking is done. The table is set.
Someone lights two candles. In an observant home, phones go off and stay off. Until three stars appear on Saturday night, there's no shopping, no work emails, no building anything.
Just meals, prayer, walks, naps, conversation. The Torah commands it, and Jewish families have kept it, stopping the world like this week after week.
A new week of the path starts here, with rest, and with the original: Shabbat.

teach.b: Shabbat comes from a Hebrew root meaning to stop, to cease. It goes back to the first pages of the Torah.
In Genesis, after six days of creation, God finishes the work, rests on the seventh day, and blesses it and makes it holy.

Later, the Ten Commandments say it plainly: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." And it isn't only for the family. The text includes servants, animals and the stranger in town: everyone gets the day.
The Torah gives two reasons, in two places.
In Exodus, the reason is creation: God rested, so you rest. In Deuteronomy, it's freedom: remember you were slaves in Egypt, and slaves never get a day off. What counts as work?
The rabbis of the Mishnah listed thirty-nine kinds, which rabbinic tradition ties to the tasks of building the sanctuary in the wilderness: sowing, baking, sewing, writing, building, kindling a fire.
What they share: they're all kinds of making.
Shabbat is a day off from making, a day for living in the world instead of changing it. The twentieth-century rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel described it as a palace built in time rather than in space.
The Jewish Sabbath has its own laws, its own prayers and its own meaning, and it belongs to the Jewish people.
This week, the path only borrows the idea underneath it, with respect: that a person needs a regular stretch where nothing has to be produced.

how: Many Jews keep Shabbat from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall, lighting candles, sharing meals and prayer, and refraining from the kinds of work Jewish law describes; practice varies across Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and secular Jews.

games.why: freedom: slaves never get a day off, so a free people rests, and gives rest to everyone in the house.

practice: Look at the week ahead and find one stretch, an evening, a morning, a few hours, where you could stop making things: no work, no errands, no fixing, no producing.
Picture how it begins, maybe with a small sign like switching off a lamp or a phone. Then picture what fills it instead: eating, walking, talking, napping.

wordCard.voice: Shabbat. Judaism's weekly day of rest, from a Hebrew root for stopping, kept from Friday sunset to Saturday night. Today's word.
